Otter Creek · Fall 2026

Our Wild
Democracy

The Story, Promise, and Future
of the Churches of Christ

All right so last week we talked about Thomas Campbell’s Declaration and Address
Quiz

What was carved on the front of the communion table in your church?

“…this do in remembrance of me.”
One click for the answer (Luke 22:19; 1 Corinthians 11:24). Let the room remember their own tables first. An invitation carved where the Seceders kept a fence: tonight is about the fence.
“Let the unity of Christians be our polar star.”
Barton W. Stone, Christian Messenger, 1832
“Resume that precious, that dear-bought liberty, wherewith Christ has made his people free…”
Thomas Campbell, Declaration and Address, 1809

Unity movement

The recap, in two founders and their own words. Stone, “An Address to the Churches of Christ” (1832), urging his churches not to divide from Campbell’s over the design of baptism; it goes on, “that the world may believe, and be saved.” In 1835: “For 32 years of my ministry I have kept in view the unity of Christians as my polar star.” Thomas Campbell, the Address (1809): “Resume that precious, that dear-bought liberty, wherewith Christ has made his people free; a liberty from subjection to any authority but his own, in matters of religion.” The same Address: “With you all we desire to unite in the bonds of an entire Christian unity.” Both opened the Lord’s table to Christians of other names: Stone at Cane Ridge, Campbell at Conemaugh.
“The Church of Christ upon earth is essentially, intentionally, and constitutionally one…”
Thomas Campbell, Declaration and Address, 1809
Unity, extending freedom of conscience to all
“We will, that this body die, be dissolved, and sink into union with the Body of Christ at large…”
The Last Will and Testament of the Springfield Presbytery, 1804
Unity, dissolving our own authority for all

Unity movement

Thomas Campbell claimed freedom of conscience and extended it to everyone; the Springfield Presbytery gave up its own authority so that every congregation could hold it.
→ “Stone’s side willed it in 1804. Tonight, the Campbells’ side does it.”
From last week

Your questions

Two questions from the room, answered in their own words. Five minutes, then into the chapter.
Question one

Did they want to include Catholics?

Short answer: yes, as Christians, though not Rome as a church. Two passages from Alexander.
One hundred millions of members

“Should any one think it lawful to paganize both the Greek and Latin churches—to eject one hundred millions of members of the Greek and Roman communions from the visible and invisible precincts of the Christian family…”

Alexander Campbell, The Christian System (1839)
• “Foundation of Christian Union,” p. 110. Read carefully: a hypothetical, not a declaration. He calls them “members” of “the Christian family”; casting them out is what “any one” might “think it lawful” to do. The sentence goes on, next slide.
Protestants only?

“…and regard the Protestant faith and people as the only true faith and the only true citizens of the kingdom of Jesus; what then shall we say of them… Of forty millions of Protestants shall we constitute the visible kingdom of the Prince of Peace? Be it so, for the sake of argument; and what then? The Christian army is forty millions strong; but how do they muster? Under forty ensigns? Under forty antagonist leaders? Would to God there were but forty!”

Alexander Campbell, The Christian System (1839)
• pp. 110–111, the same sentence. He grants the Protestants-only view only “for the sake of argument,” and even then the Protestants are no kingdom: “In the Geneva detachment alone there is almost that number of petty chiefs. My soul sickens at the details!”
• The point is division, not Rome: shut out the Greek and Roman Christians, and what remains is still at war with itself.
None among us, none in Rome

“…if there be no Christians in the Protestant sects, there are certainly none among the Romanists… and therefore no Christians in the world except ourselves… Therefore, for many centuries there has been no church of Christ, no Christians in the world; and the promises concerning the everlasting kingdom of Messiah have failed, and the gates of hell have prevailed against his church! This cannot be; and therefore there are Christians among the sects.”

Alexander Campbell, reply to a sister in Lunenburg, Virginia · Millennial Harbinger, 1837
• September 1837. A woman in Lunenburg asked how he could call unimmersed Protestants Christians. His answer runs the other way: deny them, and you must deny the Romanists too, and then the church of Christ died for “many centuries.” The centuries he means are Catholic centuries: there were Christians in them.
• The cut after “ourselves”: “or such of us as keep, or strive to keep, all the commandments of Jesus.” Same year he spent a week in Cincinnati debating Bishop Purcell against Rome as a system.
Rome, and Constantinople

“I circumscribe not the Divine philanthropy—the Divine grace. I dare not say that there is no salvation in the church of Rome, or in that of Constantinople…”

Alexander Campbell, debate with N. L. Rice, Lexington, 1843
• Printed 1844, p. 559. The sentence goes on: “though, certainly, Protestants do not regard them as churches builded upon the foundation of apostles and prophets.” So, honestly: Christians in Rome and in the Orthodox churches, yes; Rome as a church, no.
• Just before it: honest mistakes “will not… preclude any Pedo-baptist from heaven.” “The Judge of all the earth will do right.”

Christians among all the churches.
Even Rome.

Not a recognition of the Roman church as a church; a refusal to fence God’s grace. The same instinct as the token: he would not shut out those whom God had not shut out.
Question two

Unity, or uniformity?

Their answer: unity now, uniformity in God’s time, and by steps. Thomas in 1809, Alexander in 1839.
Not yet

“…nor, indeed, is there anything either in Scripture or the nature of things that should induce us to expect an entire unity of sentiment in the present imperfect state.”

Thomas Campbell, Declaration and Address (1809)
• From the Address. Unity of sentiment: everyone thinking alike. Thomas does not expect it this side of the kingdom.
But it will come

“The Church may, and we believe will, come to such a Scriptural unity of faith and practice, that there will be no schism in the body…”

Thomas Campbell, Declaration and Address (1809)
• It goes on: “no self-preferring sect of professed and acknowledged Christians rejecting and excluding their brethren. This can not be, however, till the offensive and excluding causes be removed.” And: that all should have “the same identical views of all Divinely revealed truths… appears to us morally impossible.”
Step by step

“…a still higher and more perfect degree of uniformity is intended, though neither in the first nor second instance, which are but so many steps toward it…”

Thomas Campbell, Declaration and Address (1809), the Appendix
• The steps: first, forbear with one another in love; second, stop pressing private opinions where Scripture is silent. Then, in time, “the utter abolition of those minor differences,” most of which, “had they been let alone, would have been long since dead and gone.”
• Proposition 6 says the same of inferences: they belong to “the after and progressive edification of the Church.”
Alexander, thirty years on

“Let the Bible be substituted for all human creeds; facts, for definitions; things, for words; faith, for speculation; unity of faith, for unity of opinion… and the work is done.”

Alexander Campbell, The Christian System (1839)
• “Foundation of Christian Union,” p. 115: “the whole scheme of union… in one period.” Unity of faith is the one Lord and the one confession, now. Unity of opinion is not required.

“Duty then is ours; but events belong to God.”

Thomas Campbell, Declaration and Address (1809)
• From the Address, on whether the time is right for the attempt: “whatever is to be done, must begin, some time, somewhere… if the Lord puts his hand to the work, it must surely prosper.”

Unity now.
Uniformity in God’s time.

Unity is commanded and possible today: receive one another. Agreement on everything comes, if at all, by steps and in God’s time, and is never a condition of fellowship.
→ Into tonight’s story: a young man who would not be included where others were shut out.
Our Wild Democracy · Chapter 5 · Session one

Wherever Two or Three
Are Gathered

Glasgow to Washington, Pennsylvania · 1808–1810
Matthew 18:20, and the Declaration and Address quotes it (we will see where). Chapter 5 runs two sessions. Session one: Alexander, from the shipwreck to the open table, ending beside Stone and his father. Session two: Brush Run, the ordination, and why the people.
The hour: your questions 12 · the sea 7 · Glasgow 20 · the token 6 · reunion 5 · the Synod and the reply 10 · close 6.
Philippe-Jacques de Loutherbourg, A Shipwreck off a Rocky Coast · not the Hibernia
Islay, Scotland · October 7, 1808

Alexander and the Sea

Chapter 2’s last section, which we never reached. The son’s story while the father’s is still open: his father is in America, on trial before the Seceders; Alexander, twenty, has been left in charge of the family. In Glasgow he will do, one after another, three things his father was charged with.

October 1808: the family sails

Sep 20The family sets out for Londonderry. The Hibernia is not ready; they wait eight days.
Oct 1The Hibernia sails, firing her ten cannon in farewell.
Oct 2Out into the Atlantic, then anchored again off Inishowen.
Oct 3Contrary winds off Malin Head. They run before the gale all night.
Oct 4The coast of Scotland. They anchor in Loch Indaal, on Islay, and wait for wind.
Oct 7Evening. Alexander wakes from a dream.
Six clicks; brisk until the last. Thomas had sailed ahead in 1807; now the family follows. Oct 7: Alexander dozes while reading to his sister Dorothea, and wakes alarmed: he dreamed the ship struck a rock and the water rushed in. (Richardson 1:94–99.)
October 7, evening

“I will not undress to-night. I will lay my shoes within my reach, and be ready to rise at a moment’s warning…”

Alexander Campbell, after the dream · in Richardson, Memoirs
• He told the family, and had them make ready. Let it sit before you click.
Philippe-Jacques de Loutherbourg, A Shipwreck off a Rocky Coast · not the Hibernia

That night, a gale blew in.

About ten o’clock the gale turned into the bay. The ship dragged her anchors onto a sunken rock; the water came in; they cut away the masts. No help could reach them until morning. Meanwhile his father had been tried and condemned in America, and Alexander did not know.
On the stump of the broken mast

“He thought of his father’s noble life, devoted to God and to the salvation of his fellow-beings, and felt that such a calling… was, indeed, the highest and most worthy sphere of action in which any human being could engage.”

Robert Richardson, Memoirs of Alexander Campbell (1868)
• Night, the storm still on. He sat on the stump of the broken mast, expecting to die, and thought of his father.
• → His calling is born out of admiring his father. Within months, his conscience will lead him away from his father’s church.
On the stump of the broken mast

“It was then in that solemn hour, that he gave himself up wholly to God, and resolved that, if saved from the present peril, he would certainly spend his entire life in the ministry of the gospel.”

Robert Richardson, Memoirs of Alexander Campbell (1868)
• The next sentence. Everyone survived; stranded ten months, the family wintered in Glasgow and Alexander studied at the university.
• → “Hold the mast. It comes back at the ordination.”

He had just vowed his life to his father’s calling.

In Glasgow, one by one, he did the three things his father was tried for.
One click. The irony of the winter: the son who admired his father above anyone does, without knowing it, everything the Seceders had just condemned Thomas for in Pennsylvania. Hearing other preachers; honoring laymen who preach; and, in the end, the table.
1 · Article 4 · Glasgow, winter 1808–09

He went to hear other preachers.

Above all Greville Ewing: fifteen hundred people in a converted circus.
The very thing his father was tried for: occasional hearing.
Two clicks. The family wintered in Glasgow after the wreck; Alexander studied at the university. He found the Seceder minister “a prosy speaker” and went to hear others whenever he could, above all Ewing at the Tabernacle. Back in Pennsylvania his father had been condemned for saying Seceders might hear ministers of other churches.
→ “The son is doing every week what the father was condemned for.”
With his father an ocean away

“…an effect which was, doubtless, facilitated by the fact that his revered father, to whose religious sentiments he was accustomed to pay the utmost deference, was now separated from him by the wide Atlantic.”

Robert Richardson, Memoirs of Alexander Campbell (1868)
• Richardson on what the hearing did: it released him “from the denominational influences of his religious education.” He could think for himself because his father was not in the room.
2 · Articles 2 & 3 · at Ewing’s house

Ewing told him the story of the Haldanes.

Robert and James: two brothers, sea captains turned laymen, who gave their fortune and their lives to the gospel.
One click. Robert Haldane served in the navy, James commanded an East India ship; both came home to Scotland, were converted in the 1790s, and turned everything over to preaching. James preached for years before he was ordained. Ewing had left the Church of Scotland to join them, ran their Glasgow Tabernacle, and kept the Supper weekly. His father had also been condemned for letting elders, not ministers, pray and exhort. Richardson says this story, more than anything, changed Alexander’s mind.
Robert Haldane, 1795

“Christianity… is everything or nothing. If it be true, it warrants and commands every sacrifice to promote its influence. If it be not, then let us lay aside the hypocrisy of believing it.”

Robert Haldane · in Richardson, Memoirs
• After his conversion. He resolved to give his life and his property to the gospel; his wife agreed.
A mission to India, 1797

“He accordingly determined to sell his beautiful estate of Airthrey… but, upon application to the East India Company for permission to establish the mission among the Hindoos, this was positively and unexpectedly refused.”

Robert Richardson, Memoirs of Alexander Campbell (1868)
• Inspired by William Carey in Bengal. Robert would fund the whole party, Ewing and Dr. Innes among them, with a printing press. The Company refused; appeals failed; he had already sold the estate.
The Church of Scotland on missions, 1796

“…‘That it is the duty of Christians to send the gospel to the heathen world,’ this, after debate, was voted down by a large majority — a favorite argument of the opposing party being that there was plenty of ignorance, unbelief and immorality at home…”

Robert Richardson, Memoirs of Alexander Campbell (1868)
• James Haldane was in the gallery for the debate. He knew the church was doing nothing about the unbelief at home either.

Plenty of heathen at home, the Assembly said.
So they preached at home.

From 1797 James Haldane, with lay friends, toured Scotland and the Orkneys preaching in the open air, in streets, barns and fields. Robert paid.
Their right to preach

“Whether a man… declare those important truths to two or two hundred, he is, in our opinion a preacher of the gospel…”

The Haldanes’ printed notice, 1797 · in Richardson, Memoirs
• They grounded it “upon the indispensable duty of every Christian to warn sinners.” Every Christian: the priesthood of all believers, in a Scottish handbill.
The church’s answer

“The clergy, however, soon began to manifest their hostility to lay-preaching; and the parish minister took means to deprive them of the house in which the meetings were held.”

Robert Richardson, Memoirs of Alexander Campbell (1868)
• They moved to a loft, then a barn. In 1799 the General Assembly closed the Church of Scotland’s pulpits to anyone not licensed by it.
Kintyre, 1800

“…preaching every day in the open air to large numbers. On this trip they were held for some time under arrest by the Highland chiefs, at the instigation of the clergy.”

Robert Richardson, Memoirs of Alexander Campbell (1868)
• James Haldane and John Campbell (no relation), touring Ayr, Arran and Kintyre. Richardson: “notwithstanding the opposition, great good was effected.”
• → “Refused India. Refused the pulpits. Arrested at home. For preaching.”
Their own church, Edinburgh, 1799

“The avowed object in forming this church was… to avoid that contracted spirit which would exclude from the pulpit, or from occasional communion, any faithful preacher of the gospel or sincere lover of Christ.”

Robert Richardson, Memoirs of Alexander Campbell (1868)
• Pushed out, the Haldanes formed a church whose first rule was not to push anyone out. Three hundred and ten joined at once. Ewing drew up its plan of government.
• → “A church built on refusing to exclude. Alexander is sitting at that man’s table.”
What he saw in the churches

“He was particularly impressed with the persistent opposition of the clergy… and the disposition they constantly manifested to exercise the power which they possessed in an arbitrary manner.”

Robert Richardson, Memoirs of Alexander Campbell (1868)
• The same sentence: “the unscrupulous methods they often resorted to to hinder the progress of the truths they refused to admit.” The corruption he saw was the use of power to shut people out.
Alexander, looking back

“imbibed disgust at the popular schemes, chiefly while a student at Glasgow.”

Alexander Campbell, in after years · in Richardson, Memoirs
• Richardson sets it against “the course which the clergy pursued under the influence of their narrow policies and bigoted sectarianism.”

He was welcome at his church’s table.

Ewing was not.

The Haldanes were not.

Two clicks. The Seceder table was for Seceders in good standing, with a token. The men whose preaching and piety he most admired could not have sat at it.

Can you be included by a church that excludes?

Ask the room, and wait. Then carry it into his struggle: what he came to want, and what held him.
What he came to want

“…the principles of Congregationalism entertained by Mr. Ewing, which secured an entire emancipation from the control of domineering Synods and General Assemblies…”

Robert Richardson, Memoirs of Alexander Campbell (1868)
• “…and which seemed to him much more accordant with primitive usage.” The congregation free of the church courts: the seed of tonight.
But it was his father’s church

“…he did not feel himself at liberty to abandon rashly the cherished religious sentiments of his youth, and the Seceder Church to which his father and the family belonged…”

Robert Richardson, Memoirs of Alexander Campbell (1868)
• The same page as “domineering Synods.” Everything pulled him toward Ewing’s freedom; everything he loved held him to his father’s church, where “he had thought it his duty to be a regular communicant.”
• Call back the mast: the boy who vowed his life to his father’s ministry.
3 · The table · Glasgow, spring 1809

The communion season came. He was examined, and given the token.

Eight hundred communicants, eight or nine tables. He waited for the last one.
One click. The Seceder church’s spring communion. No letter from Ireland, so the elders examined him and gave him the lead token, his ticket to the table.
Why he waited

“His conscientious misgivings as to the propriety of sanctioning any longer, by participation, a religious system which he disapproved, and, on the other hand, his sincere desire to comply with all his religious obligations, created a serious conflict in his mind, from which he found it impossible to escape.”

Robert Richardson, Memoirs of Alexander Campbell (1868)
• Taking part would put his stamp on the system; leaving would break with his father’s church. He waited for the last table “in hopes of being able to overcome his scruples.” He wanted to stay.
• Hit the word sanctioning. His father, leaving the Seceders in America, would use the same word.

“…the ring of the token, falling upon the plate, announced the instant at which he renounced Presbyterianism for ever — the leaden voucher becoming thus a token not of communion but of separation.”

Robert Richardson, Memoirs of Alexander Campbell (1868)
• When the plate came round he dropped the token on it, and when the bread and wine came down the table he “declined to partake.” He told no one.
• → Silence. Do not explain it.

Welcomed at a table that turned others away,
he gave back the token.

The answer to the question, in an act rather than a word. Richardson: he was “unable any longer conscientiously to recognize the Seceder Church as the Church of Christ.”

Family Reunion

October 1809. The family finally lands in Philadelphia and crosses the mountains.
October 1809 · the road into Washington, Pennsylvania

Thomas rode out to meet them.

On the ride back he told his son everything: the trial, the rebuke, and that he had left the Seceders.
One click. Apart two and a half years. Alexander had carried his decision alone for six months, and expected his father to oppose him.
On the road, 1809

“…instead of fearing opposition from him to the views to which he had himself been definitely brought while in Glasgow, he found him already, though by a somewhat different method, led practically to the very same conclusions.”

Richardson, Memoirs 1:220
• He lands in the autumn of 1809, crosses the mountains, and meets his father on the road. Thomas has just written the Declaration and Address, and Alexander reads it in proof.
• → “Father and son, an ocean apart, arrive at the same place.”

The father opened the table to people who had no token.

The son held a valid token, and would not use it.
Neither knew.
Two clicks. Say it plain and stop.
The father had been tried for serving the Supper to Presbyterians of other kinds in 1807; the son had walked away from a fenced table in 1809.
That fall they asked him to write down what they stood for

“The Church of Christ upon earth is essentially, intentionally, and constitutionally one; consisting of all those in every place that profess their faith in Christ…”

Thomas Campbell, Declaration and Address (1809)
• Chapter 3: the Declaration and Address, which Alexander read in proof that autumn. Optional sting: the presbytery formally deposed Thomas on April 18, 1810, seven months after it was published.
The Brush Run meeting house, reconstructed at Bethany · courtesy of Bethany College
1810–1811

Brush Run

A creek and a few farms, about eight miles from Washington. The meeting house was a plain frame building, never finished; it was later sold, moved, used as a blacksmith shop, a post office and a barn, and rebuilt at Bethany in 1909.

“This Society by no means considers itself a Church, nor does at all assume to itself the powers peculiar to such a society…”

Thomas Campbell, Declaration and Address (1809), Resolution IV
• What they promised in 1809: “merely as voluntary advocates for Church reformation.” A society can preach; it cannot keep the Supper or ordain.
• → “Now they would have to be one.”
But a society is not a church

“…as the Society was not a Church… most of its members… were deprived of various privileges which belonged to the church relation.”

Robert Richardson, Memoirs of Alexander Campbell (1868)
• No Lord’s Supper, no baptism, no ordination: a society can preach, but it cannot keep the table. Most members had drifted from their old congregations; some had never belonged to any.

“…the Society must obtain admission into some regularly organized religious body, or be itself compelled to change its attitude and resolve itself into an independent Church — an alternative which Thomas Campbell particularly desired to avoid.”

Robert Richardson, Memoirs of Alexander Campbell (1868)
• The Society’s first plan was not to become a church at all. In October 1810 Thomas asked the Presbyterian Synod of Pittsburg, a body other than the Seceders who had tried him, to receive him and the Association.
The Synod of Pittsburg, October 1810

“…Mr. Campbell’s request to be received into ministerial and Christian communion cannot be granted.”

Minutes of the Synod of Pittsburg, October 1810 · in Richardson, Memoirs
• Unanimous. Among its reasons: Thomas’s “opposing creeds and confessions as injurious to the interests of religion.” Then the reasons, and Alexander’s November reply.
The “important reasons,” October 5
“for expressing his belief that there are some opinions taught in our Confession of Faith which are not founded in the Bible”
“for declaring that the administration of baptism to infants is not authorized by scriptural precept or example”
“for encouraging or countenancing his son to preach the gospel without any regular authority”
“for opposing creeds and confessions as injurious to the interests of religion”
Minutes of the Synod of Pittsburg, October 1810 · in Richardson, Memoirs
Four clicks. Thomas came back the next day and asked what the “important reasons” were. The fourth is tonight’s: a creed used as a test of communion is a fence at the table, and he would not keep one. He said he felt “quite relieved”: none of it was for immorality.
→ “The Synod would not have him because he would not shut anyone out. Alexander answered three weeks later.”
Alexander answers, November 1810

Who may come?

Alexander’s reply to the Synod, an address to the Christian Association on November 1, 1810: the creeds as gates, Gabriel, the “party man” address, and the gates as wide as heaven. This is the token, put into words: the position the Synod had just refused.
The creeds as gates

“That standards had been lifted up which narrowed the gates of Zion… and there were none of them but would reject those whom God has not rejected, and deny admission to those whom God had admitted.”

Alexander Campbell, address to the Christian Association, November 1810 · in Richardson, Memoirs
• “Standards” are the confessions used as tests of admission. His text was Isaiah 62:10, “go through the gates.”

“All are defective. The apostle Paul, the angel Gabriel in human form, could not be admitted on the principles of these standards.”

Alexander Campbell, November 1810 · in Richardson, Memoirs
• Let the room laugh. Then: the Seceder table he walked away from in Glasgow would not have had the apostle, and neither would the Synod of Pittsburg.
Why he would join no party

“I dare not be a party man for these reasons… Because no party will receive into communion all whom God would receive into heaven.”

Alexander Campbell, 1810 · in Richardson, Memoirs
• The same year: an address after a sermon at Mr. Buchanan’s. The next line: “God loves his children more than our creeds, and man was not made for the Bible, but the Bible for man.”
• Chapter 1’s table and Chapter 2’s trial, in one sentence.
The gates of admission

“We have decided, therefore,… to open the gates of admission into the Church as wide as the gates of heaven.”

Alexander Campbell, November 1810 · in Richardson, Memoirs
• In full: “to lift it up as a standard for the Church,” the New Testament as the only test of admission. The same address: the Society’s first work was “to remove the stumbling-block of making the private opinions of men a term of communion.”
Side path · creeds as tests

Creeds may teach. May they exclude?

Side path. The Campbells did not reject creeds as teaching; they rejected them as tests of fellowship, because a test shuts out people God has not shut out. Thomas Campbell, 1809.
Proposition 7

“That although doctrinal exhibitions of the great system of Divine truths, and defensive testimonies in opposition to prevailing errors, be highly expedient, and the more full and explicit they be for those purposes, the better; yet… they ought not to be made terms of Christian communion…”

Thomas Campbell, Declaration and Address (1809)
• Confessions are good teaching. They are human reasoning, full of “inferential truths,” so they cannot be the door.
Proposition 7, continued

“…unless we suppose, what is contrary to fact, that none have a right to the communion of the Church, but such as possess a very clear and decisive judgment… whereas the Church from the beginning did, and ever will, consist of little children and young men, as well as fathers.”

Thomas Campbell, Declaration and Address (1809)
• The reason: a test of doctrine excludes the young in faith, whom God has not excluded. 1 John 2:12–14.
Proposition 6

“…yet are they not formally binding upon the consciences of Christians farther than they perceive the connection… Therefore, no such deductions can be made terms of communion, but do properly belong to the after and progressive edification of the Church.”

Thomas Campbell, Declaration and Address (1809)
• Inferences belong to teaching, “the after and progressive edification of the Church,” not to admission.

Creeds may teach.
They may not fence the table.

Back to the spine: the token, in words.

In Glasgow he gave back the token.

In Washington he said why.
One click. Spring 1809, a lead token on a plate; November 1810, “as wide as the gates of heaven.” The same refusal, eighteen months apart: he would not be included by a table that excluded. And it is the position that kept his father out of the Synod.
Three founders, one table
Barton Stone, 1803: withdrew from the Synod’s “jurisdiction, but not from their communion”
Thomas Campbell, 1807: tried for serving the Supper to Presbyterians outside the Seceders
Alexander Campbell, 1809: gave back the token
Three clicks, one founder each. Stone, Chapter 4: suspended from the Synod’s jurisdiction, he would not break communion with it (Stone, Biography, ch. VII). Thomas, Chapter 2: the 1807 charge. Alexander, tonight. Three men, three countries of origin, none knowing the others’ story, each broken with his church over who may come to the table.

Three founders.
One open table.

End of the first act. Alexander stands beside Stone and his father: an idealist who would not be included where others were shut out. End of session one: discussion and the idea follow.

Idea

The Lord’s table
turns no Christian away.

Glasgow: the Haldanes’ church was formed to “avoid that contracted spirit which would exclude”; the Seceder table would not have had them. Alexander gave back the token. In 1810: no standard should “reject those whom God has not rejected.” Brush Run kept the table open to every Christian.

And they make their own minister.

Quiz

Which is the preferred title for our preacher?

A.Pastor
B.Reverend
C.Brother←
D.None of the above
One click points to C. Let the room argue first; “none of the above” (minister, evangelist, preacher) is a fair answer too.
• Not “Reverend”: the Last Will willed that title “be forgotten” (last week). Not “Pastor”: in the New Testament the pastors are the elders.

Wherever Two or Three

Brush Run, Pennsylvania · 1811–1812
Session two. Recap in one breath: the shipwreck, the Haldanes, the token given back, father and son meeting on the road, the Synod’s refusal, the gates as wide as heaven. Three founders, one open table. Tonight: what the Campbells did once every body they asked had refused them, and who made their minister.
The hour: Brush Run 8 · the first Supper 5 · the ordination 6 · why the people 17 · close 8.
Last session

Three founders.
One open table.

Last session’s last card. Stone in 1803, Thomas in 1807, Alexander in 1809: each broke with his church over who may come to the table.
→ “Refused by the Synod, the Campbells still had no church. Two ways not to become a sect.”

Two ways not to become a sect

The pattern to highlight. Both sides feared becoming one more party. Stone’s presbytery solved it by dissolving itself. The Campbells tried to solve it by joining a body that already existed, and kept trying.
Stone’s side, 1804 · dissolve our own body

“We will, that this body die, be dissolved, and sink into union with the Body of Christ at large…”

The Last Will and Testament
The Campbells’ side, 1810 · join an existing one

“…the Society must obtain admission into some regularly organized religious body…”

Richardson, Memoirs
One click. The same fear, opposite remedies. Thomas left the Seceders and set out to join another body; what follows is that attempt, and its refusal. Even after Brush Run became a church, they kept looking for a body to join (side path: Becoming Baptists).
Side path · becoming Baptists · Brush Run’s overture, fall 1813

“…expressing a willingness, upon certain conditions, to co-operate or to unite with that Association, provided always that we should be allowed to teach and preach whatever we learned from the Holy Scriptures, regardless of any creed or formula in Christendom.”

Alexander Campbell, Millennial Harbinger 1848 · in Richardson, Memoirs
• Side path, two years ahead. After the Campbells were immersed in 1812, Baptist congregations for sixty miles around asked Alexander to preach and “all pressed us to join their Redstone Association.” Brush Run’s answer: eight or ten pages, “exhibiting our remonstrance against all human creeds as bonds of communion.” The Association voted, “by a considerable majority,” to receive them: “Thus a union was formed.”
The name of his paper, 1823

“As the reformers were, however, at this time identified with the Baptists, it was thought expedient, in order to avoid offending religious prejudice… to make this concession so far as the name of the paper was concerned, qualifying “Baptist” by the word “Christian.””

Richardson, Memoirs, vol. 2
• The Christian Baptist, 1823–1830. Richardson calls it a concession; it was also simply true: the reformers were Baptists. He had debated as the Baptist champion against John Walker (1820) and W. L. Maccalla (1823).
• In 1829 he dropped the name because “he feared that the name Christian Baptists would be given to the advocates of the Reformation.” The 1848 memory was written from the far side of that break.

Refused by the Presbyterians,
they became Baptists.

For most of the next two decades the Campbells’ churches belonged to Baptist associations: Redstone from 1813, Alexander’s Wellsburg church in the Mahoning Association from 1823. His paper (1823–1830) was called The Christian Baptist. The separation came around 1830.
→ “Stone gave up his institution. The Campbells kept looking for one to belong to.”
Why a church

“…on account of the continued hostility of the different parties, it was necessary that the Christian Association should assume the character of an independent Church, in order to the enjoyment of those privileges and the performance of those duties which belong to the Church relation.”

Robert Richardson, Memoirs of Alexander Campbell (1868)
• The pastoral need. Its members had been shut out or had drifted from their old congregations: no Supper, no baptism for their children, no one to marry or bury them.
Thomas Campbell, spring 1811

“It was with great reluctance that he finally concluded to take this step, and to separate himself from those whom he desired to recognize as brethren.”

Robert Richardson, Memoirs of Alexander Campbell (1868)
• Spring 1811. Every overture refused, Thomas concluded “that the Christian Association should assume the character of an independent Church.” The thing he had dreaded since 1809. “At the next meeting of the Association, accordingly, the matter was duly considered and agreed to.”
May 4, 1811

Brush Run Church Formed

Saturday, May 4, 1811, at the Brush Run meeting house. About thirty members. They sang Psalm 118 in the old Scottish metrical version.

No bishop. No presbytery.
A congregation.

Let it sit. This is the thing no church court could imagine: a church that makes its own ministers.
Brush Run · May 5, 1811

The First Supper

The next day, May 5, 1811, the new church kept the Lord’s Supper for the first time. Alexander preached.
His sermon

“I am that bread of life.”

John 6:48 · Alexander’s text that morning · in Richardson, Memoirs
• And verse 58: “He that eateth of this bread shall live for ever.” Two years after he left a table with his token unused, he preaches at a table of his own.
The sermon’s close

“…in assembling there on that occasion, they furnished an emblem of the millennial state of the Church, nay, an emblem of the heavenly state, when men of different nations, and known by different names, should sit down together in the kingdom of God.”

Alexander Campbell’s communion sermon · in Richardson, Memoirs
The high point of the hour. His text: John 6:48, “I am that bread of life.” Richardson is summarizing his sermon notes.
→ “The table is not only a memory. It is the future, arriving early: everyone who will be at the last table, at this one.” Chapter 1’s table, again.
Every Lord’s day

“…the Lord’s Supper, which, according to the custom of the Independent churches in Scotland, was now celebrated weekly.”

Robert Richardson, Memoirs of Alexander Campbell (1868)
• The Haldane churches again. At Cane Ridge the Supper came once or twice a year, after weeks of preparation and a token. At Brush Run, every Sunday, from the beginning. That is us.
Every Lord’s day · a resource

The table every Lord’s day

The early church, the Reformers, Wesley, Rome,
the ecumenical movement, and Brush Run
A resource. Weekly communion is not a Church of Christ peculiarity: it is the oldest practice of the church, which almost every tradition has said it wants back. Every quote is in the document “Every Lord’s day.”
The early church

“But every Lord’s day gather yourselves together, and break bread, and give thanksgiving…”

The Didache 14 (c. 100)
• A church manual from about the end of the first century. The sentence goes on: “after having confessed your transgressions, that your sacrifice may be pure.”
c. 155

“And on the day called Sunday… bread and wine and water are brought, and the president in like manner offers prayers and thanksgivings, according to his ability, and the people assent, saying Amen…”

Justin Martyr, First Apology 67 (c. 155)
• Every Sunday, in Rome. “According to his ability”: no fixed prayer. And the people’s Amen is part of the act.
The Reformers

“Each week, at least, the table of the Lord ought to have been spread for the company of Christians…”

John Calvin, Institutes 4.17.46
• Calvin wanted it and never got it: Geneva’s council held him to quarterly communion. The same section calls once-a-year communion “an invention of the devil.”
Wesley

“I also advise the elders to administer the Supper of the Lord on every Lord’s Day.”

John Wesley to the American Methodists, 1784
• His letter sending the first Methodist elders to America. (The Wesley Corpus calls its transcription provisional.)
The table every Lord’s day
“…the Lord’s Supper… was now celebrated weekly.” Brush Run, 1811 · Richardson, Memoirs
“As the eucharist celebrates the resurrection of Christ, it is appropriate that it should take place at least every Sunday.” Baptism, Eucharist and Ministry (1982), Eucharist 31
Two clicks. A congregation by a creek in 1811, and the ecumenical movement in 1982, arriving at the same table.
Rome, on us

“It came from the desire to lead the Church towards a unity rooted in the weekly celebration of the Lord’s Supper.”

Disciples of Christ–Roman Catholic dialogue, The Church as Communion in Christ (1992)
• The Catholic Church’s own dialogue with the Disciples, describing the Stone-Campbell movement. A study document, not official teaching on either side.

“This phase of the dialogue has achieved consensus that the weekly celebration of the Eucharist is fundamental to an understanding of the Christian life…”

Disciples–Catholic dialogue, Do This in Memory of Me (2018)
• The same report: the Disciples’ weekly Supper, “inclusive in practice,” “has had a significant influence on their determined effort to work for Christian unity.” Honest limit: the Catholic table is still closed to Disciples.

The whole church has asked for it.
Brush Run kept it.

The end. → Back to the spine.

Who serves the table?

Side path: who may serve? Brush Run kept the Supper every Lord’s day, open to every Christian. Campbell’s argument goes further: the table is kept by the priesthood of all believers.
The same priesthood keeps the table

“May they not, without a human priest to consecrate the way for them, approach the Lord’s table, and handle the loaf and cup?”

Alexander Campbell, The Christian System (1839), “Breaking the Loaf”
• Later, in The Christian System. The sentence before: “May not, then, holy and royal priests thank God for the Lord’s table, its loaf, and cup of wine?”
• He had already written, in the Christian Baptist (1827): “‘The administration of ordinances’ is a popish phrase, and ought to be cashiered from the christian vocabulary.”

“…the royal priesthood may approach the Lord’s table without fear, inasmuch as they are consecrated to officiate by a blood…”

Alexander Campbell, The Christian System (1839), “Breaking the Loaf”
• Consecrated to officiate: not by a bishop’s hands, by Christ’s blood. Every baptized member is ordained to the table.
• Against the clergyman who says “Stand by, I am holier than thou”: he “desecrates the royal priesthood of Jesus Christ.”

“…he that gives thanks for the loaf should break it not as the representative of the Lord, but after his example… And thus they as priests feast upon his sacrifice.”

Alexander Campbell, The Christian System (1839), “Breaking the Loaf”
• Between the two halves: the disciples hand the loaf “to one another,” and the one who broke it eats with them. No one stands in for Christ; everyone serves everyone.
• → In our congregations the thanks at the table are given by members, not by the preacher. That is this, still.
Throwback · Thomas Campbell, 1809

“That division among the Christians is a horrid evil, fraught with many evils. It is antichristian, as it destroys the visible unity of the body of Christ…”

Thomas Campbell, Declaration and Address (1809), Proposition 10
• Chapter 3. The table is where that unity is shown, or denied: a fenced table divides the body at the very place it is meant to be one.
Before us

“…where three are, a church is, albeit they be laics.”

Tertullian, On Exhortation to Chastity 7 (c. 210)
• The sentence before: where there is no clergy, “you offer, and baptize, and are priest, alone for yourself.” Tertullian is echoing Matthew 18:20. The old church knew the thought; it did not keep it.
Scotland

“The apparent question at issue was: may a group of believers not set in order with a presbytery eat the Lord’s Supper or not?”

D. B. Murray, on the Scotch Baptists, Baptist Quarterly (1989)
• The Scottish independents the Campbells knew in Glasgow were split on exactly this. Glasites and strict Scotch Baptists: no Supper without an elder. The Glasgow Scotch Baptists divided over “eating without elders” in 1810, the year after Alexander left. The British Churches of Christ grew from the side that ate without elders.
Two or three

“…were only two christians in any place, such as on shipboard… they ought to commemorate the death of Christ on the first day of the week…”

Ballantine’s Essays on the Elder’s Office, reprinted in Stone’s Christian Messenger (1835)
• The ground: “our Lord gives directions, Mat. xviii. 15—20. to the smallest number that might thus meet in his name.” Two or three gathered are a church, and a church keeps the Supper. (Recall Alexander on the Hibernia.)

“Is there any thing to be done at the table of the Lord, which any brother, who can give thanks for a crucified Savior, and repeat the words of the institution, cannot do?”

The same essay, in Stone’s Christian Messenger (1835)
• It goes on: to suppose “that none but an Elder can administer the Supper” attributes “some sanctity and power to an Elder which the scriptures do not warrant.” Printed in Barton Stone’s own paper.
Campbell

“‘The administration of ordinances’ is a popish phrase, and ought to be cashiered from the christian vocabulary.”

Alexander Campbell, The Christian Baptist (1827)
• Answering a reader. He goes on: persons the church appoints, “when attending their respective duties,” are “administering all the ordinances.” The church’s appointment is what gives “an official right”; no sacred power passes through it.
The test of a clergy

“He would not tolerate a disciple in his church to baptize a candidate, nor to ‘administer the Lord’s supper,’ nor to pray over the loaf or the cup.”

Alexander Campbell, Millennial Harbinger (1830)
• His proof that a preacher belongs to “the aspiring priesthood”: he will not let an ordinary disciple give thanks at the table. If he does permit it, Campbell says, “I will except him from the priesthood.”
Campbell’s model church

From his memorandum book

In The Christian System, “Breaking the Loaf,” Campbell copies a Lord’s day he saw in an unnamed congregation (“The church in ——”), as “the highest approach to the model, which we have in our eye.” Not Brush Run, so far as we know; written in the 1830s. Who presided at Brush Run in 1811 is not recorded.
Who presided

“Not having any person whom they regarded as filling Paul’s outlines of a bishop, they had appointed two senior members, of a very grave deportment, to preside in their meetings. These persons were not competent to labor in the word and teaching; but they were qualified to rule well…”

Alexander Campbell, The Christian System (1839), “Breaking the Loaf”
• About fifty members. No ordained man, and none needed: the church appointed two of its own. “One of them presided at each meeting.”
Every member a part
“He then called upon a brother… to read a section of the evangelical history.”
“…the president called upon a brother to pray in the name of the congregation.”
“…the whole congregation, brethren and sisters, pronounced aloud the final Amen.”
Alexander Campbell, The Christian System (1839), “Breaking the Loaf”
Three clicks. The president calls on members; the members read, pray and answer. A brother also names the hymn before the table.
At the table
“…he took a small loaf from the table, and in one or two periods gave thanks for it.”
“…each one waiting upon his brother, until all were served.”
Alexander Campbell, The Christian System (1839), “Breaking the Loaf”
Two clicks. The loaf passed “from one to another”: “no stiffness, no formality, no pageantry; all was easy, familiar, solemn, cheerful.” Campbell’s picture of the ancient order at the table.
Campbell’s verdict

“There was no stiffness, no formality, no pageantry; all was easy, familiar, solemn, cheerful.”

Alexander Campbell, The Christian System (1839), “Breaking the Loaf”
• And: the thanksgivings were as brief “as the thanks usually presented at a common table.” Honest note: “the strangers sat off on seats more remote”; in this church the bread and cup went to the disciples.
His qualifier

“He may of right preach, baptize, and dispense the supper, as well as pray for all men, when circumstances demand it.”

Alexander Campbell, The Christian System (1839)
• Of every Christian. But: “This concession does not… authorize any individual to assume to do what has been given in charge to them” (the appointed officers). “Liberty without licentiousness, and government without tyranny.” In 1840: “Official grace and official virtue are the very essence of popery.”
Stone’s Christians

“For you cannot find in the New Testament one instance of the church having authority to ordain elders or bishops or deacons, or to administer baptism or the supper. You will find that the ministry existed before the church…”

Stone’s Christian Messenger (1830)
• Attributed to Stone by the Messenger’s index. The Christians ordained their elders, kept the Supper seldom, and held that the ordained should administer it. The exact opposite of “the fountain of official power.”
The union, 1832

“…they believe that no person but a preacher has a right to administer the ordinances — such as the breaking of the loaf…”

A letter from Lexington, Kentucky, February 1832 · Millennial Harbinger
• The month after Stone and “Raccoon” John Smith shook hands in Lexington. A local union of Christians and Reformers broke up over this: whether a church without an ordained preacher could break the loaf. They “become very much alarmed at the idea of uncommon folks receiving the name of kings and priests to the Lord.”

“When he is absent the church can do nothing. Like a widow forlorn and desolate, she is solitary and silent.”

Alexander Campbell, “The Union,” Millennial Harbinger (1832)
• Campbell’s reply, about the preacher “called and sent… to administer ordinances”: make him indispensable and the congregation cannot even meet at its own table.
The Churches of Christ settle it

“One, of course, leads in giving thanks. This is not officiating, for any disciple can do this. It does not pertain to any office.”

David Lipscomb, Queries and Answers (1910)
• Lipscomb (Gospel Advocate, Nashville): “The elders, or those who preside, can call on any disciple to do this. He only expresses aloud and leads in what every disciple does.” Our practice: members give thanks at the table; the elders arrange it.
Three paths from one table
“An ordained minister, as representative of Christ presiding at the Lord’s Table, serves in Christ’s place as host at the Table.” Disciples–Catholic dialogue, 2009
“…within Australian Churches of Christ ‘lay presidency’ is almost the norm…” Churches of Christ in Australia to the World Council, 1986
“…we have denied women the opportunity to pass Communion trays because we have described it as a ‘leadership role.’” David Kneip, Siburt Institute, ACU, 2025
Three clicks. The Disciples, in dialogue with Rome, came back to the minister as Christ’s representative; Campbell had said the one who breaks the loaf does so “not as the representative of the Lord, but after his example.” Australia kept mutual ministry. Our churches kept “any disciple” but read it as “any man,” and now argue whether passing a tray is leadership or service. In 2020 every household became its own table.

Open to all.
Hosted by any.

Brush Run’s table was weekly and its fences were coming down. Campbell’s argument goes further: the table is kept by the priesthood of all believers. Not only open; hosted by any.
January 1, 1812

The Ordination

Licensed in May 1811; ordained on January 1, 1812. He preached all over the region through 1811 and married Margaret Brown that March. At Christmas he sat down, as he did every year’s end, to examine himself.
May 4, 1811

“At this meeting, Thomas Campbell was appointed elder, and Alexander was licensed to preach the gospel. Four deacons were also chosen…”

Robert Richardson, Memoirs of Alexander Campbell (1868)
• The deacons: John Dawson, George Sharp, William Gilcrist, James Foster. About thirty members.
• No presbytery licensed him. The church did.
December 25, 1811 · his own list
“Special instances of Divine power which I consider to bind me under obligations to be specially devoted to Him…
III. In resolving, when in imminent danger at sea, to serve God in this way, on two occasions of extraordinary deliverance…
XI. In giving me a call from the Church to preach the Gospel…
XII. In my desire to suffer hardships and reproach in that good work.”
Alexander Campbell · in Richardson, Memoirs
Three clicks. Twelve reasons; three shown. The mast comes back: “two occasions” are the Hibernia off Islay in 1808, and the 1809 crossing on the Latonia, which sprang a leak and nearly went down in a squall.
Number XI: the call came from the church, not from a court.

“We do hereby certify that Alexander Campbell… was, according to the principles of this Church regularly chosen and ordained a minister thereof, upon the first day of January, one thousand eight hundred and twelve.”

Certificate of ordination, recorded in the Brooke County court, December 1812 · in Richardson, Memoirs
• He needed it in court to be allowed to perform marriages. Signed at a church meeting at John Dawson’s, September 1, 1812.
• The cut: “after a due course of trials preparatory to the work of the holy ministry.”
Signed
Thomas Campbell, senior minister
George Sharp · William Gilcrist · James Foster · John Dawson, deacons
The ordination certificate · in Richardson, Memoirs
One click. His father, and four farmers. One of them, James Foster, is the man nearly kept out by the test question. The man who would debate Robert Owen and the Catholic bishop of Cincinnati, and found a college, was ordained by a creekside congregation of about thirty.
The meaning of January 1, 1812

Why the people?

The theory behind the ordination: why Brush Run believed the authority to make a minister was its own.
A witness, 1520–1523

Martin Luther: ordained in baptism

Three centuries before Brush Run. The ground of the whole argument: the authority is given in baptism, to every Christian; the congregation’s call decides who uses it. Baptismal succession.
Luther

“…all Christians are truly of the ‘spiritual estate,’ and there is among them no difference at all but that of office…”

Martin Luther, To the Christian Nobility (1520)
• The sentence before: “It is pure invention that pope, bishops, priests and monks are to be called the ‘spiritual estate’; princes, lords, artisans, and farmers the ‘temporal estate.’”
Ordained in baptism

“For whoever comes out the water of baptism can boast that he is already consecrated priest, bishop and pope…”

Martin Luther, To the Christian Nobility (1520)
• And: “Through baptism all of us are consecrated to the priesthood, as St. Peter says in I Peter 2:9.” A minister is one of the priests, chosen by the rest: “as though ten brothers, all king’s sons and equal heirs, were to choose one of themselves to rule the inheritance for them all.”

“…we are all priests, and there is no difference between us; that is to say, we have the same power in respect to the Word and all the sacraments. However, no one may make use of this power except by the consent of the community…”

Martin Luther, The Babylonian Captivity of the Church (1520)
• The whole sentence ends “or by the call of a superior.” Every Christian has the power; the community’s call decides who uses it. Brush Run’s logic, three centuries early.
1523

“…no one can deny that every Christian has God’s Word and is taught of God and anointed by Him to the priesthood.”

Martin Luther (1523)
• From the treatise for the congregation at Leisnig, defending its right to call its own pastor.
Luther, 1523

“If the bishop does not confirm him, he is none the less confirmed by virtue of the call of the congregation.”

Martin Luther (1523)
• Luther wrote it and later settled for princes running the church. Brush Run, three centuries on, did it.
Luther, 1523 · for the congregation at Leisnig
“…the sheep are to judge whether what they teach is the voice of Christ or the voice of strangers.”
“All teachers should and must, therefore, be subject with their teaching to the judgment of the hearers.”
Martin Luther, That a Christian Assembly or Congregation Has the Right and Power to Judge All Teaching and to Call, Appoint, and Dismiss Teachers (1523)
Two clicks. Leisnig had dismissed the priest its patron appointed and elected its own. Luther: “If the bishop does not confirm him, he is none the less confirmed by virtue of the call of the congregation.” Later he settled for princes running the church. Our preachers answer to the congregation: this is why.

“You see that ordination is not a mere unmeaning thing, but consists in the choice of the people, which must be hearty…”

Alexander Campbell, sermon on Titus 1:5 · in Richardson, Memoirs
• His notes for a sermon that winter. The sentence goes on: “and that it might be evidenced, the elders or rulers impose their hands.” The authority is the congregation’s: two or three gathered, each a priest by baptism.
Church government · a resource

Who governs the church?

What Jesus said, what Cane Ridge willed,
and what Brush Run did.
A resource, to take when the room asks. The sources run in order: Matthew 18, the priesthood texts, the Declaration and Address on Matthew 18, the Witnesses’ Address and the Last Will, Alexander Campbell.
To the gathered church

“…tell it unto the church: but if he neglect to hear the church, let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican. Verily I say unto you, Whatsoever ye shall bind on earth shall be bound in heaven…”

Matthew 18:17–18 (KJV)
• In Matthew 16:19 the keys go to Peter. Here the binding and loosing go to “the church”: the gathering that hears a brother’s trespass. The next verses: two who agree; two or three gathered.

“For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them.”

Matthew 18:20 (KJV)
• The Declaration and Address quotes it to the friends of reform: “Let not the paucity of your number… prove an insuperable discouragement.”
Thomas Campbell on Matthew 18 · Appendix

“‘What ye bind on earth shall be bound in heaven’ is the awful sanction of the Church’s judgment, in justly rejecting any person. Take away this, and it has no sanction at all.”

Thomas Campbell, Declaration and Address (1809)
• Matthew 18:18 gives the church’s verdict heaven’s weight. So to cast someone out over an opinion is to pronounce him lost: “Does he not henceforth become to us as a heathen man and a publican?” The weight is why the church must not spend it on opinions.

“An individual church or congregation of Christ’s disciples is the only ecclesiastical body recognized in the New Testament. Such a society is ‘the highest court of Christ’ on earth.”

Alexander Campbell, Christian Baptist, July 5, 1824
• From “Essays on Ecclesiastical Characters, Councils, Creeds, and Sects, No. III.” Every session, presbytery, synod, assembly or conference that legislates or rules “essentially becomes ‘the man of sin and the son of perdition.’” He then reprints Alexander Carson on Matthew 18: “Here the last appeal is to the church. He does not say, If he does not hear the church, take him to the presbytery…”
Every believer
“But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people…” 1 Peter 2:9 (KJV)
“And hath made us kings and priests unto God and his Father…” Revelation 1:6 (KJV)
Two clicks. Said of the whole church, not of an order within it. Richardson’s note on Alexander’s reply cites both.

“…they soon found that there was neither precept nor example in the New Testament for such confederacies as modern Church Sessions, Presbyteries, Synods, General Assemblies, etc.”

The Witnesses’ Address, appended to the Last Will and Testament, 1804
• Researching a book on church government, the Springfield Presbytery found that it was itself one of these confederacies; it dissolved itself.

“Why do we contend for uninterrupted succession in ordination, seeing it is not the persons called bishops who have the power, but the people?”

Alexander Campbell · in Richardson, Memoirs, sermon on Titus 1:5
• Brush Run, winter 1811–12. The same sermon: ordination “consists in the choice of the people, which must be hearty.”
Asked why he preached without authority
“Who has authority?
Who gave the Presbytery authority to license men?
Who gave the Presbytery authority to make laws for the Church?
Who gave the Presbytery authority to decide religious matters by vote?
Who gave the Presbytery authority to choose ministers?”
Alexander Campbell · in Richardson, Memoirs
Four clicks; the question keeps extending. End of the side path. He turns the charge around: the presbytery is the one without authority.
What the hands do

“As to the form or ceremony of ordination, he did not regard it as conferring any authority, but as a public testimony that the persons ordained possessed the necessary authority.”

Robert Richardson, Memoirs of Alexander Campbell (1868)
• Side path. The second way our tradition narrates its ordinations: no authority is conferred, because none is needed. It resolves into the first: none is needed only because the authority was already given, to every Christian, in baptism. Baptismal succession: Luther, “whatever issues from baptism may boast that it has been consecrated priest, bishop, and pope.” Richardson goes on: he “utterly repudiated the claim of apostolic succession.”

Christ in the midst of two or three.
Every other office answers to that.

The end of the resource. → Back to the spine.
The Springfield Presbytery, 1804 · the court gives up its power
“We will, that our power of making laws for the government of the church, and executing them by delegated authority, forever cease…”
“We will, that candidates for the Gospel ministry… obtain license from God to preach the simple Gospel…”
The Last Will and Testament of the Springfield Presbytery
One click. Chapter 4, Cane Ridge: the presbytery dissolved itself. Two items about ministers: the presbytery will no longer license anyone; a minister’s license comes from God.
The Springfield Presbytery, 1804 · the congregation takes it up
“We will, that the church of Christ assume her native right of internal government—try her candidates for the ministry… and admit no other proof of their authority, but Christ speaking in them.”
“We will, that each particular church, as a body… choose her own preacher… and never henceforth delegate her right of government to any man or set of men whatever.”
The Last Will and Testament of the Springfield Presbytery
One click. Where the authority goes: to each congregation. Seven years later and hundreds of miles away, a congregation that never heard of the will tried its own candidate, licensed him in May 1811 and ordained him in January 1812.

The Springfield Presbytery died
so that congregations could choose.
Brush Run chose.

Neither side knew the other existed. The two streams meet in 1832; they already agreed.
His views, 1811

“Each church was independent, and had the exclusive authority to select its own officials, who were, when approved, to be set apart by a formal ordination.”

Robert Richardson, Memoirs of Alexander Campbell (1868)
• Richardson: “These views he continued to maintain unchanged through life.”

“The clergy are the opposite to the laity. Both these terms are used in Scripture to denote God’s people. Trace them to their origin and we find no difference.”

Alexander Campbell, reply to the Synod, November 1810
• Clergy from klêros, the Lord’s lot or inheritance; laity from laos, the people of God. Both words name the whole church.
Alexander, later

“The community, the church, the multitude of the faithful, are the fountain of official power. This power descends from the body itself — not from its servants. Servants made by servants are servants of servants…”

Alexander Campbell, The Christian System (1839)
• The theory of Brush Run, written down twenty-seven years later. It goes on: authority “thus derived from Christ the head, immediately through his body,” is surer than one “derived through a long, doubtful, corrupt dynasty of bishops or pontiffs.”
The whole church remembers · a resource

What the whole church knows

The priesthood of all · the consent of all
baptism that unites
A resource. The claim: the Church of Christ stands for what is most universal in the church, and is distinctive only where others have let one of these slip. Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and ecumenical voices, in their own words. Every quote is in the document “The whole church.”
The priesthood of all

“The New Testament never uses the term ‘priesthood’ or ‘priest’ (hiereus) to designate the ordained ministry… the term is reserved… for the unique priesthood of Jesus Christ and… for the royal and prophetic priesthood of all baptized.”

World Council of Churches, Baptism, Eucharist and Ministry (1982), Ministry 17
• The Lima text: the most widely studied ecumenical document of the century, drafted by a commission that included Catholic and Orthodox theologians.
Orthodox

“The gift of the Spirit that every member of the faithful receives in the sacrament of initiation is the charism of royal priesthood.”

Nicolas Afanasiev, The Church of the Holy Spirit, p. 3
• A Russian Orthodox theologian in Paris (d. 1966). His second chapter is titled “The Ordination of Laics”: every baptized Christian is ordained.
Orthodox

“The first, the basic definition of man is that he is the priest.”

Alexander Schmemann, For the Life of the World (1963)
• Not of clergy: of every human being, who receives the world from God and offers it back. The same book: “Religion is needed where there is a wall of separation between God and man. But Christ… has broken down the wall… He has inaugurated a new life, not a new religion.” (Page to verify against the book.)
The governance of all

“…I made up my mind to do nothing on my own private opinion, without your advice and without the consent of the people.”

Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, c. 250
• A bishop of the third century, to his clergy, on how he had governed from the beginning.

“He who is to govern all, should be chosen by all.”

Leo the Great, bishop of Rome, Letter 10 (444)
• The next sentence: “The consent of the clergy, the testimony of those held in honour, the approval of the orders and the laity should be required.” A pope.
Orthodox

“…the protector of religion is the very body of the Church, even the people themselves…”

Encyclical of the Eastern Patriarchs (1848)
• The four Orthodox patriarchs, answering Pius IX: neither patriarchs nor councils could introduce novelties, because the people guard the faith. And at every Orthodox ordination the people still shout Axios!, “He is worthy!”, the trace of the time when the whole church chose.
Catholic

“…in this Church, as in an inverted pyramid, the top is located beneath the base. Consequently, those who exercise authority are called ‘ministers’, because, in the original meaning of the word, they are the least of all.”

Pope Francis, October 17, 2015
• The same address quotes “a principle dear to the Church of the first millennium”: quod omnes tangit ab omnibus tractari debet, what touches all should be discussed by all.
Why it is beautiful

“Juridical power is a substitute for love in actual social life… In the Church, where perfect love dwells, there is no need for such a substitute.”

Nicolas Afanasiev, The Church of the Holy Spirit, p. 274
• The case for congregational governance is not a legal one. Where love governs, the apparatus of power is unnecessary.
Baptism · the Synod on Synodality, 2024
“There is nothing higher than this baptismal dignity, equally bestowed upon each person…”
“…as well as constituting the basis of synodality, Baptism is also the foundation of ecumenism.”
Final Document of the Synod on Synodality, October 26, 2024, §21, §23
Two clicks. Received by Pope Francis as part of his ordinary teaching. Baptism, not ordination, as the root of the church’s life and of its unity.
Baptism

“Our common baptism, which unites us to Christ in faith, is thus a basic bond of unity.”

World Council of Churches, Baptism, Eucharist and Ministry (1982), Baptism 6
• Baptism as what unites. Where baptism becomes a fence, a universal has slipped.

“To the intent that now unto the principalities and powers in heavenly places might be known by the church the manifold wisdom of God…”

Ephesians 3:10 (KJV)
• The church exists to show something. Our practices (no clergy class, members at the table, the congregation choosing, everyone singing) are testimony as much as order: a small visible demonstration of what the whole church confesses.

What the whole church confesses,
we try to practice every Lord’s day.

The end of the resource. Distinctive only where others let a universal slip. → Back to the spine.
The church as ekklēsia · a resource

The word Paul chose
was the name of the citizens’ assembly

A resource. In every Greek city Paul visited, ekklēsia was the regular meeting of the citizens: the body that heard, debated and voted. Paul named the churches with that word. Scholars now argue the democratic overtones were deliberate; others trace the word to the Greek Old Testament’s word for Israel’s assembly (qahal). Both are assemblies of the whole people. Every quote is in the document “The assembly.”
Athens: the open floor

“Freedom’s mark is also seen in this: Who hath wholesome counsel to declare unto the state?… What greater equality can there be in a city?”

Euripides, Suppliants (c. 423 BC), trans. Coleridge
• Theseus, defending democracy to a king’s herald. The line echoes what the herald cried at every Athenian assembly: Tis agoreuein bouletai?, “Who wishes to speak?” Any citizen could stand. Demosthenes remembers the morning Philip of Macedon took Elatea: “the marshal put the question, Who wishes to speak? No one came forward.” He calls that cry “the civic voice of our country.”
• All citizens over twenty could attend; votes were by show of hands. “Citizens” meant adult men only: women, slaves and foreigners were shut out.
The same word, in the New Testament

“…it shall be determined in a legal congregation… And when he had said these things, he dismissed the congregation.”

Acts 19:39–41 · The Living Oracles, Alexander Campbell’s New Testament (1826)
• The riot at Ephesus. The town clerk sends the mob home and points them to the city’s regular assembly. Luke calls both the mob and the lawful assembly ekklēsia. Campbell’s New Testament gives the civic assembly and the church one English word: congregation.
The scholars

“…Paul wished to portray his communities as alternative organizations existing alongside the civic assemblies… in many respects, the functioning of the Christian ekklēsia mirrors the operations of the civic assemblies.”

George H. van Kooten, New Testament Studies (2012)
• Van Kooten (Groningen, now Cambridge). Anna C. Miller, Corinthian Democracy (2015): the Corinthians understood themselves as “a powerful, democratic assembly.” Philip Esler, who thinks the word came from the Greek Old Testament, still says Paul’s churches took on the connotations of “civic voting assemblies.”
The Christian assembly

“When you are come together, each of you has a psalm, has a discourse, has a foreign language, has a revelation, has an interpretation!”

1 Corinthians 14:26 · The Living Oracles, Alexander Campbell’s New Testament (1826)
• Not a herald asking who wishes to speak: the Spirit has given every member something to bring. “To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit” (12:7).
The floor passes · 1 Corinthians 14:29–31
“…and let the others judge.”
“…you can all prophesy, one by one,”
“…that all may learn, and all may be comforted.”
The Living Oracles, Alexander Campbell’s New Testament (1826)
Three clicks. Speakers take turns; the gathered body weighs what is said. And the verse before: “if to another, sitting by, any thing be revealed, let the first be silent.” The floor passes. Caution: 14:34–35 silences women, against 11:5 where they pray and prophesy; many scholars think those verses were added later.
The assembly decides
“…this punishment, which was inflicted by the majority.” 2 Corinthians 2:6
“…who was also chosen by the congregations our fellow-traveller.” 2 Corinthians 8:19
The Living Oracles, Alexander Campbell’s New Testament (1826)
Two clicks. A vote, and an election. The Greek for “chosen” in 8:19 is cheirotonētheis, literally “by stretching out the hand”: the word for electing by show of hands. Esler: 2:6 “takes us straight into the dynamics of the political ekklēsia as a voting assembly.”
The translators’ fight

“…where I found this word ecclesia, I interpreted it by this word congregation.”

William Tyndale, answering Thomas More (1531)
• Tyndale’s reason: the clergy had taken for themselves “the term that of right is common unto all the whole congregation of them that believe in Christ.” More attacked him for it. King James’s rules for the 1611 translators, rule 3: “the Word Churche not to be translated Congregation.”
Campbell takes Tyndale’s side

“Wherever the word church is found in the common version, congregation will be found in this.”

Alexander Campbell, appendix to the Living Oracles
• His reason: “The term church, or kirk, is an abbreviation of the word kyriou oikos, the house of the Lord, and does not translate the term ekklēsia.” In 1824 he had printed Alexander Carson’s gloss: the Greeks, “particularly the Athenians,” used it “for their popular assemblies… in which none but citizens had a right to sit.”
And back again

“…modern democracy began with the experience of the Puritan congregations.”

A. D. Lindsay, The Modern Democratic State (1943)
• A political philosopher (Master of Balliol, Oxford), seeing it from the other direction: the self-governing congregation as the seedbed of modern democracy. The ekklēsia took the city’s word; the city later learned from the congregation.

Not a building. Not a clergy.
The people, assembled.

The end of the resource. Ekklēsia names the gathering, every member with a voice, under Christ. → Back to the spine.
Confession or constitution · a resource

What governs the church?

The Westminster Confession, and the Declaration and Address
A resource, split from “Church government.” Two answers: a confession that puts the keys in the hands of officers, and Thomas Campbell’s New Testament as the church’s whole constitution, with many local congregations and one church.
The other answer · Westminster Confession, chapter 30
30.1 “The Lord Jesus, as King and Head of his church, hath therein appointed a government, in the hand of church officers…”
30.2 “To these officers the keys of the kingdom of heaven are committed…”
Westminster Confession of Faith, American text (1788)
Two clicks. Of Church Censures. Matthew 18 gives the binding and loosing to the church; Westminster gives the keys to its officers. Richardson: Thomas Campbell, applying to the Synod of Pittsburg, accepted the Confession “with the exception that… [he] objected to the chapter conferring power upon the clergy.”
Proposition 4

“…the New Testament is as perfect a constitution for the worship, discipline, and government of the New Testament Church… as the Old Testament was for the worship, discipline, and government of the Old Testament Church…”

Thomas Campbell, Declaration and Address (1809)
• The constitution is the New Testament. Nothing written since governs the church.
Proposition 2

“That although the Church of Christ upon earth must necessarily exist in particular and distinct societies, locally separate one from another, yet there ought to be no schisms, no uncharitable divisions among them.”

Thomas Campbell, Declaration and Address (1809)
• Local congregations, many; one church. The locality is natural; the division is the sin.

Not a confession over the church.
The New Testament is its constitution.

The end of the resource. → Back to the spine.

A minister, made by
the priesthood of all believers.

The meaning Brush Run attached to it: the authority to make a minister is in the congregation, because every member is a priest. Luther said it first: whoever comes out of the water of baptism is already priest, bishop and pope.
Black.
◆ for discussion · session two

What is beautiful here? What do we carry forward?

Backup prompts (off the slide): Who gives thanks at our table, and why that person? Who has authority in our congregation, and where did it come from? What would it mean to believe every member could be called?
Idea 1 of 2

The church can gather
for those who are shut out.

Brush Run became a church because its people were refused “those privileges… which belong to the Church relation.” No synod granted it; the people constituted it, with great reluctance, for each other’s sake.
Idea 2 of 2

The priesthood of all believers
makes its ministers.

Ordination “consists in the choice of the people”: the two or three gathered hold the priesthood’s authority, given in baptism. Brush Run did what the Last Will bequeathed. “The community, the church, the multitude of the faithful, are the fountain of official power.” No clergy-laity line. Side paths: who may ordain?; who may serve?; the whole church remembers.
Chapter 5’s ideas
1.The Lord’s table turns no Christian away.
2.The church can gather for those who are shut out.
3.The priesthood of all believers makes its ministers.
The chapter’s three ideas at once, both sessions, before the discussion.
